candidateDecisions.label: Europe's diversity, borders, belonging and migration
candidateDecisions.reason: Modern History and sociology address migration, nationalism and belonging. Human Rights and EU Law add legal dimensions of rights and movement. Media & Race and histories of empire offer substantive perspectives on exclusion, often outside Europe. These are valuable supports, but a third plan would rely on the same Europe-focused core without a sustained sequence on European migration, borders and belonging.

analysis: The closest option directly covers EU politics, legislation and legal reasoning. Comparative institutions, global modern history and empires give social and historical context; introductory and public economics and macroeconomics provide distinct tools for market policy and public institutions. Sociology and political philosophy address civil society and authority, while qualitative and quantitative methods, source-based historical inquiry and negotiation build research and policy practice. Dutch contributes basic language study. The climate option combines climate physics, environmental risk, life-cycle accounting and renewable design with policy, law, governance and environmental justice. Climate communication studies public debate and representations, while Persuasive Communication applies framing and persuasion in sustainability projects and asks students to evaluate their practice. Description-only risk, renewable design, environmental justice, history research and climate communication support concrete roles within the documented scope. The two options share 14 courses and add ten each. Migration, rights and belonging have meaningful supporting courses, including modern history, migrant solidarity in social theory, human rights and EU movement law. The available further history and media courses largely study non-European settings and the dedicated European institutional coursework is already in the closest plan. This does not sustain a third focused sequence in European migration and borders.

alignment.rationale: Both study modern political orders and changes in sovereignty and national identity. UCR takes a global view from 1815 onward, while Maastricht centres Europe and starts with the French Revolution.

Both train students to work critically with historical sources in research. Back to the Sources is a shorter skills component, while the History Research Seminar runs the full research cycle from research question to a substantial research paper.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Imagining Europe studies the development of European identities; UCR has no course on European identity or culture, and Modern History, which touches national self-determination, is placed with Ruling Europe.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Lifting the Iron Curtain is a regional course on Central and Eastern Europe after communism; no scheduled UCR course addresses that region, and Modern History is placed with Ruling Europe.

Both study the actors, institutions and decision-making rules of the EU and the approaches used to study EU politics. Constructing Europe also develops theory and challenges of integration across a full course, while European Union Politics is a single course.
Both introduce the main theories of international relations and apply them to contemporary issues and actors. Theory of International Relations has a global rather than European focus.

Both teach negotiation as a practised skill through simulation and role-play. Negotiation Skills is tied to European and international settings, while Negotiation & Strategic Thinking teaches negotiation in general.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: European Diplomacy in the 21st Century studies EU external action and diplomatic practice; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart, and Theory of International Relations is placed with Globalizing World.

Both introduce the legal order of the EU and its institutions. Ordering Europe is a full course on the autonomous EU legal order and is followed by EU Law II, whereas UCR offers a single foundations course.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: EU Law II is a second EU-law course; UCR offers a single EU-law course, which is placed with Ordering Europe.
UCR supplies macroeconomic tools for analysing policy, growth and international interdependence. Maastricht applies international economics to European integration.

Both address the relationship between market and state in economic policy. Public Economics analyses market failure, public goods, taxation and political economy in general terms, while Governing the European Economy applies the question to the EU.
Both introduce quantitative research methods, including research design, surveys and descriptive and inferential statistics.
Both introduce qualitative research methods, including formulating questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small research projects.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Working with Research Problems is a programme-specific skills module on handling research problems in European Studies; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart beyond the methods courses placed elsewhere.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: The Academic Workshop I is a seven-EC skills workshop specific to the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Exploring Contemporary Challenges is the first part of the three-part Academic Workshop II in the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Discussing Contemporary Challenges is the second part of the three-part Academic Workshop II in the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Publishing about Contemporary Challenges is the seven-EC final part of Academic Workshop II in the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Research Methods: Interviewing is a four-EC skills module on interview research for thesis students; no scheduled UCR course teaches interviewing, and Qualitative Research Methodology is placed with Introduction to Qualitative Methods.
This Maastricht route requires a 17 EC thesis and a separate 4 EC methods course. UCR displays optional independent research alongside the thesis.

Both develop core academic skills: Personal & Professional Development teaches students to select and critically analyse sources, formulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments, and improve writing and speaking, which is an important part of the function of Research and Writing in European Studies; the UCR course is broader and not specific to European Studies.
Both are language-learning courses. Students of European Studies choose a second language at the Language Centre, and Dutch is a beginner language course at UCR.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the one-EC Student Support Programme is a year-long support module within the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.
The 24 EC elective semester can include a minor, exchange, an internship or approved electives.
